title: Venus and Adonis
description: Shakespeare's first published work, a 1,194-line Ovidian epyllion dedicated to the Earl of Southampton: the goddess Venus courts the boy Adonis, who scorns her for the hunt; her warnings of the boar come true, and the poem ends with the flower sprung from his blood and Venus's prophecy of love's future sorrows.
plot_or_argument: Venus plucks Adonis from his horse and pleads her love through the day's rhetoric of desire; he resists, breaks away at dawn, and is killed by the boar; Venus finds the body, curses love, and transforms the youth into the purple flower she plucks and cradles.
narrative_structure: A single erotic episode expanded by debate, digression, and the two great set pieces of the horse and the hunted hare, framed by the myth's metamorphosis.
meter_and_prosody: Six-line stanzas (ababcc) of iambic pentameter — the 'Venus and Adonis stanza' — of unexampled sensuous polish.
historical_context: Printed by Richard Field in 1593, during the plague closure of the theatres; it was Shakespeare's best-seller, reprinted some fifteen times by 1636, and advertised by Francis Meres in 1598 as proof of 'sugared' Shakespeare's wit.
literary_significance: The founding text of the English Ovidian vogue of the 1590s and the first of the two narrative poems on which Shakespeare staked his poetic fame.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; published with Shakespeare's name on the title page.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Field, 1593. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: The Rape of Lucrece
description: Shakespeare's second narrative poem, also dedicated to Southampton: the Roman matron Lucrece is raped by Tarquin, the king's son, who steals into her chamber at Collatium; her night-long debate with grief ends in her public accusation and suicide before husband, father, and the Roman lords, whose vengeance expels the Tarquins and founds the republic.
plot_or_argument: Tarquin, inflamed by Collatine's praise of his wife, rides to Collatium, is welcomed, and violates Lucrece in her bed; her apostrophes to Night, Opportunity, and Time occupy the central lament; at dawn she summons her kin, names her ravisher, and stabs herself; Brutus casts off his feigned simplicity and leads Rome to revolt.
narrative_structure: A three-movement structure — Tarquin's inward debate before the deed, Lucrece's grief after it, and the public consequence — composed as a series of rhetorical set pieces in the complaint tradition.
principal_characters: Lucrece; Tarquin; Collatine; Lucretius; Brutus; the Nurse
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal (ababbcc), in a graver, more deliberative music than Venus and Adonis.
historical_context: Printed by Richard Field in 1594; its matter — the violation that founds a state — draws on Ovid's Fasti and Livy, and its political ending (the expulsion of tyrants) spoke to the succession anxieties of the 1590s.
literary_significance: The deepest of the Elizabethan complaint poems — a study of trauma, rhetoric, and political consequence that anticipates the great tragedies.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Field, 1594. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).

title: Shakespeare's Sonnets
description: The 154 sonnets printed in 1609, with the long poem 'A Lover's Complaint' appended: a sequence to a beautiful young man urging him to marry and immortalizing him in verse, shadowed by a rival poet and by the 'dark lady' of the later sonnets — the greatest sonnet collection in the language, and the most argued-over book of poems in English literary history.
plot_or_argument: The first seventeen sonnets press the youth to marry; the middle poems anatomize love, jealousy, absence, and the rival poet; the dark lady sequence (127–152) turns on lust and self-betrayal; and the final poems rework Cupid and the cures of love, closing with 'A Lover's Complaint' spoken by a forsaken maid.
narrative_structure: A sequence of 154 sonnets with a detectable narrative arc — courtship, crisis, self-reproach — followed by the appended complaint.
principal_characters: the poet; the young man (Fair Youth); the dark lady; the rival poet; the maid (in the Complaint)
meter_and_prosody: The Shakespearean sonnet (abab cdcd efef gg) brought to its definitive form, with 'A Lover's Complaint' in rhyme royal.
historical_context: Composed across the 1590s and early 1600s, partly circulating in manuscript; printed by Thomas Thorpe in 1609 with the dedication 'To the onlie begetter of these insuing sonnets, Mr. W.H.' — the most famous crux in English bibliography.
literary_significance: The summit of the English sonnet tradition; its identities, erotic shapes, and textual mysteries have made it a permanent site of scholarship and dispute.
attribution_notes: Uncontested as Shakespeare's; the identities of the Fair Youth, the dark lady, and 'Mr. W.H.' remain unknown.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Thomas Thorpe, 1609. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005); Katherine Duncan-Jones (ed.), Shakespeare's Sonnets (Arden, 1997).

title: The Phoenix and the Turtle
description: Shakespeare's 67-line metaphysical elegy, printed in Robert Chester's collection Love's Martyr (1601) alongside poems by Jonson, Chapman, and Marston: the funeral of the phoenix and the turtle dove, whose chaste love united them 'in a mutual flame', leaving reason itself to compose the threne over their urn.
plot_or_argument: The birds assemble for the obsequies; the anthem declares the lovers one in essence, 'two distincts, division none'; reason, confounded, speaks the threne; and the poem closes on the paradoxes of truth and beauty buried with them.
narrative_structure: A tripartite ceremony — summons, anthem, threne — in the form of a compressed metaphysical emblem poem.
principal_characters: the Phoenix; the Turtle; Reason; the assembled birds
meter_and_prosody: Trochaic tetrameter with the irregular 'threne' in trimeter — the most deliberately 'metaphysical' verse Shakespeare wrote.
historical_context: Published in 1601 as an appendix to Chester's Love's Martyr, dedicated to Sir John Salusbury; its allegorical referents (Salusbury's circle, the Earl of Essex, or pure emblem) remain undetermined.
literary_significance: The strangest and most debated of Shakespeare's poems — the one place where he joins the metaphysical company of Donne.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in Robert Chester, Love's Martyr, 1601. Standard edition: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition (2005).
